title: Pytheas of Massalia's voyage to Britain and Thule
summary: Around 330 BCE Pytheas set out from the Greek city of Massalia (modern Marseille) and reached Britain, where accounts place him at the tin-producing area Belerion, believed to be Cornwall, and at Kent. He also reported Thule, an island about six days' sail north of Britain, which scholars identify as Iceland or Norway.

uncertainty.note: World History Encyclopedia says he embarked sometime around 330 BCE and that his account was written in Greek around 325 BCE; Diller gives 330 BCE as his floruit. Years are astronomical (330 BCE = -329, 325 BCE = -324). The id year -325 follows the account date.

as_recorded.value: Written in Greek sometime around 325 BCE

where.modern_name: Marseille, France (Massalia; Britain lies on the route)
where.historical_name: Massalia, a Greek city on the coast of Gaul

waypoints.label: Massalia (modern Marseille): generally accepted as the start of his voyage.
Belerion, tin-mining site believed to be Cornwall. Point is the centre of the historic county.
Kantion, the Kentish peninsula named in the account. Point is the centre of the county.

importance.justification: Earliest reported Greek exploration of Britain and the far north; the account is known through later authors.

sources.title: On the Ocean: The Famous Voyage of Pytheas
sources.author: Thomas S. Garlinghouse

sources.title: Pytheas of Massalia (Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography)
sources.author: Aubrey Diller

beats.caption: Pytheas sails from Massalia to Britain, noting the tin-working area of Belerion and the Kentish peninsula.
His account, written in Greek around 325 BCE, describes Thule as an island six days north of Britain.
Scholars still disagree on where Thule lay: the usual view is Iceland, but some argue for Norway.

reviewer_note: Least sure: Thule is deliberately not pinned because its identification is debated (Iceland usual, Norway argued). Route order is the order named in the source, not a dated itinerary. Belerion/Cornwall is a belief per World History Encyclopedia; Cornwall and Kent points are county centres.
